name: TypeScript
description: TypeScript is JavaScript with static types that help catch mistakes during development, improve editor support, and make larger codebases easier to maintain.

blocks.html:
Introduction & Setup

What is TypeScript?

TypeScript is JavaScript with a static type-checking system. It helps you find mistakes while writing code, such as passing the wrong kind of value to a function or misspelling an object property. TypeScript checks code before it runs, rather than waiting for a bug to appear while a user is using the application.

TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript: valid JavaScript syntax is generally valid TypeScript, and TypeScript adds types and other development-time features. Types are erased during compilation; the generated JavaScript is what browsers and Node.js execute.

Type checking versus running

The compiler can report type errors, but it does not guarantee that your program is bug-free. Runtime errors, incorrect logic, invalid data from an API, and many other problems still need testing and validation.

Install and create a project

You need Node.js and npm. In a terminal, run:

mkdir hello-ts
cd hello-ts
npm init -y
npm install -D typescript
npx tsc --version

-D installs TypeScript as a development dependency. npx runs the local compiler without requiring a global installation.

Create your first TypeScript file

Save this as hello.ts. The annotations : string and : number describe the expected values.

Compile and run it:

npx tsc hello.ts
node hello.js

The compiler creates a JavaScript file. Node.js runs that JavaScript—not the TypeScript types.

tsconfig.json

For a project, initialize a configuration file:

npx tsc --init

Common compiler settings:

OptionPurpose
targetJavaScript language version to output
moduleModule format used for generated code
strictEnables stronger type checking
rootDirWhere source files are located
outDirWhere compiled JavaScript is written
noEmitCheck types without generating JavaScript
sourceMapCreates maps that help debug generated code
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2020",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "strict": true,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist"
  }
}

When a project has a tsconfig.json, run npx tsc to compile using its settings, or npx tsc --noEmit to type-check only.

Common mistakes

  • Trying to run a .ts file directly with Node without a supported TypeScript runtime setup.
  • Editing generated JavaScript instead of the TypeScript source.
  • Assuming type checking catches every runtime bug.
  • Leaving strict checking disabled in a new project without a reason.

Key points

  • TypeScript adds static checking to JavaScript.
  • The compiler checks types and emits JavaScript.
  • Types are not normally present at runtime.
  • tsconfig.json controls compiler behavior.

Basic Types & Type Inference

Primitive types

Use lowercase primitive type names. string represents text, number represents integer or decimal numbers, and boolean represents true or false.

TypeExample
string"Hello"
number10, 3.14, -5
booleantrue, false
nullnull
undefinedundefined
bigint100n
symbolSymbol("id")

Type inference

Type inference means TypeScript determines a variable's type from its initial value. You do not need to annotate every simple variable. Once inferred, assigning an incompatible value produces a type error.

any and unknown

any disables type checking for a value and should be avoided when possible. unknown can hold any value, but you must narrow or validate it before using it safely.

TypeAccepts any value?Use without checking?
anyYesYes (checking is bypassed)
unknownYesNo

Literal types and const

Literal types restrict a value to an exact value. A const variable can often be inferred as a literal type, while a let variable is usually inferred as a wider type. Use as const to preserve literal values in an object or array.

Common mistakes & key points

  • Use lowercase string, number and boolean, not wrapper object types.
  • Do not use any casually.
  • Inference often removes the need for explicit annotations.
  • Literal types restrict values to exact choices.
  • Types help during development; runtime data still needs validation.

Arrays, Tuples & Enums

Typed arrays

An array normally contains values of the same type. Use type[] or Array<type>. TypeScript checks the values you insert and access.

Tuples

A tuple describes an array with a known number of positions and a type for each position. It is useful for small structured values such as coordinates or key-value pairs. Tuple types can include optional or rest elements.

Enums

Enums name a set of related constant values. Numeric enums start at zero by default and increment. String enums use explicit readable string values. In many modern projects, string literal unions or as const objects are also common alternatives.

Readonly arrays

readonly T[] or ReadonlyArray<T> prevents array mutation through that typed reference. It is a compile-time restriction, not a guarantee that the underlying array is frozen at runtime.

Key points

  • Use number[] and string[] for typed arrays.
  • Tuples type each position and their intended length.
  • Enums name a fixed set of values; string enums are readable in output.
  • Readonly array types stop mutation through that reference.

Typing Functions

Parameter and return types

Type each parameter and optionally specify the return type after the closing parenthesis. The compiler checks calls and returned values. Return types can often be inferred, but explicit annotations are helpful for public functions and learning.

Optional and default parameters

A parameter is required unless marked optional with ? or given a default value. Optional parameters must come after required parameters. A default parameter can be omitted at the call site.

void and never

void is used for functions that do not return a useful value. never describes values or functions that cannot complete normally, such as a function that always throws or an exhaustive branch that should be impossible.

Function types and callbacks

You can describe a function's shape and use it for callback parameters. This helps make callback arguments and results predictable.

Function overloads

Overloads describe multiple allowed call signatures for a function. The implementation must support all overloads. They are useful when different input types produce specific result types.

Common mistakes & key points

  • Calling a function with the wrong argument type or count.
  • Putting optional parameters before required ones.
  • Forgetting a return value when a function promises one.
  • void means no useful return; never means no normal completion.
  • Use function types for callbacks and overloads for distinct call signatures.

Objects, Interfaces & Type Aliases

Object types

Object types describe which properties an object has and their types. Required properties must exist. Optional properties use ?. You can also use readonly properties to prevent reassignment through that typed reference.

Interfaces

An interface describes the shape of an object and can be extended by another interface. Interfaces are commonly used to describe objects, class contracts, and data structures.

Type aliases

The type keyword gives a name to a type. Type aliases can describe object shapes, unions, intersections, tuples, primitives, and function types. Unlike interfaces, aliases cannot be reopened for declaration merging.

Index signatures

An index signature allows an object to have keys of a particular type and values of another type. Use it when the set of property names is not known ahead of time, such as a dictionary.

Interface versus type

Featureinterfacetype
Object shapeYesYes
Extend/combineextends& intersection
UnionNoYes
Declaration mergingYesNo

Rule of thumb: use interfaces for object contracts; use type aliases when naming unions, intersections, tuples, or other types. Either can describe object shapes.

Common mistakes & key points

  • Missing required properties.
  • Optional properties may be undefined; check before using them.
  • readonly is a compile-time restriction, not runtime immutability.
  • Use interfaces to describe object contracts and aliases for flexible type expressions.

Union, Intersection & Narrowing

Union types

A union (A | B) means a value may be one of several types. Literal unions restrict values to specific choices and are useful for status values, directions, and options.

Narrowing with typeof

With a union, you can only use operations that are safe for every member. Narrowing means checking the value to learn which member it is before using member-specific features. Use typeof for primitive values.

Narrowing with in and instanceof

The in operator checks whether an object has a property. instanceof checks whether an object is an instance of a constructor, such as a built-in class.

Intersection types

An intersection (A & B) combines requirements from both types. A value must satisfy all intersected types.

Discriminated unions

Object unions can share a literal property such as kind. Checking that property tells TypeScript which object variant you have. This is an especially useful pattern for app states and API results.

Custom type guards

A user-defined type guard is a function whose return type uses value is SomeType. It tells TypeScript how a successful check narrows the value.

Common mistakes & key points

  • Calling methods on a union before narrowing it.
  • typeof results are lowercase strings such as "string".
  • Use in, instanceof, equality checks, or custom guards to narrow.
  • Union means OR; intersection means satisfy BOTH.
  • Discriminated unions make branching over object variants safer.

Classes, Inheritance & Access Modifiers

Classes and constructors

A class defines a blueprint for objects. TypeScript allows you to type fields, constructor parameters, methods, and control access to members.

ModifierMeaning
publicAccessible anywhere (default)
privateAccessible only inside that class
protectedAccessible inside the class and subclasses
readonlyCannot be reassigned after initialization/constructor

Parameter properties

Adding public, private, protected, or readonly to constructor parameters creates class properties automatically. This is a convenient shortcut.

blocks.output: Sadia teaches Databases Sadia leads Databases

blocks.html:
Inheritance and overriding

A class can extend another class and inherit its members. A subclass can override a method to provide a specialized implementation. Use super to call the parent constructor or method.

Implementing interfaces

A class can use implements to promise it follows an interface. The compiler checks that it contains the required properties and methods.

Getters and setters

Accessors let you expose a property-like interface while controlling how values are read or changed. Validate values inside setters when needed.

Common mistakes & key points

  • Trying to access a private member outside its class.
  • Remember: protected can be accessed by subclasses, but not by unrelated outside code.
  • Use extends for inheritance and implements for interface contracts.
  • Parameter properties create fields automatically.
  • TypeScript's private is a compile-time restriction; JavaScript's #private fields provide runtime privacy.

Generics

Why generics?

Generics let you write reusable code while preserving the type of the data. Instead of repeating a function for different types or using any, use a type parameter such as T. TypeScript infers the type parameter from the arguments in many cases.

Explicit type arguments

Inference usually works, but you can explicitly provide a generic type argument when useful.

Generic constraints

Use extends to restrict the types that a generic can accept. For example, a function using .length can require that its input has a numeric length property.

Generic interfaces and classes

Generic types can be used with interfaces, type aliases, and classes. This is useful for reusable containers, API response shapes, and collections.

Default generic parameters

A generic type can provide a default type parameter. If a caller does not specify a type and inference cannot choose one, the default is used.

Common mistakes & key points

  • Using any instead of a generic loses type safety.
  • Using properties of T without a constraint.
  • Type parameters are placeholders, not runtime variables.
  • TypeScript infers generic types from arguments.
  • T extends X sets a constraint; it does not mean T must be exactly X.

Utility Types & Modules

Built-in utility types

Utility types transform existing types so you can reuse object shapes rather than duplicate them.

UtilityPurpose
Partial<T>Makes all properties optional
Required<T>Makes all properties required
Pick<T, K>Selects specified properties
Omit<T, K>Removes specified properties
Readonly<T>Makes properties readonly
Record<K, V>Creates keys K with values V
Exclude<T, U>Removes U from union T
Extract<T, U>Keeps members of T assignable to U
ReturnType<F>Gets a function's return type
Parameters<F>Gets a function's parameter tuple

keyof, typeof and indexed access

keyof creates a union of an object's property names. Type-level typeof obtains the type of an existing value. Indexed access types use T[K] to look up a property's type.

Modules: export and import

Modules organize code into files. Export values or types from one file and import them in another. Named exports are imported using braces; a default export is imported without braces. A file with top-level import or export is treated as a module.

// math.ts
export interface Result {
  value: number;
}

export function add(a: number, b: number): Result {
  return { value: a + b };
}

export default function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a * b;
}

// main.ts
import multiply, { add, type Result } from "./math";

const result: Result = add(2, 3);
console.log(result.value, multiply(2, 3));

Enums and alternatives

Enums can represent a finite set of named choices. String enums are readable when logged. In many codebases, literal unions or as const objects are used instead because they are simple and work naturally with JavaScript.

Common mistakes & key points

  • Partial is useful for update objects, but it can make required data optional.
  • Readonly is compile-time only.
  • Named imports must match exported names.
  • Use import type for type-only imports when appropriate.
  • Utility types, keyof, typeof, and indexed access help derive types from existing definitions.

topics.title: Null Safety, Assertions, Async & Practical TypeScript

blocks.html:
Null Safety, Assertions, Async & Practical TypeScript

null, undefined and strict checks

With strictNullChecks enabled (included by strict), null and undefined are separate types. A value that may be missing must be checked before it is used.

Optional chaining and nullish coalescing

Optional chaining (?.) safely accesses a property or calls a method when the value may be nullish. Nullish coalescing (??) supplies a fallback only for null or undefined, unlike ||, which also treats zero, false, and empty strings as falsy.

Type assertions and satisfies

A type assertion tells TypeScript how you intend to treat a value. It does not convert the value or validate it at runtime. Use assertions only when you have stronger knowledge than the compiler. The satisfies operator checks that a value conforms to a type while preserving its more specific inferred type.

Async functions and Promises

An async function returns a Promise. Write the resolved value's type in the function's return type as Promise<T>. Use await to read the resolved value inside an async function.

Error handling

In a catch block, the caught value is typed as unknown under strict settings. Check whether it is an Error before accessing its message. External data should also be validated before trusting it.

DOM typing

TypeScript includes browser DOM types. A query may return null if no element is found, so check it before use. Use a generic with querySelector to describe the element type when appropriate.

Practical type-checking workflow

In an application, define the types for your data, validate external input, use strict compiler settings, and type-check regularly. Types alone do not validate JSON received from a server.

npx tsc --noEmit

Example API response shape:

interface ApiUser {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

interface ApiResponse<T> {
  success: boolean;
  data: T;
}

Common mistakes & final key points

  • Using ! or assertions to silence errors without checking reality.
  • Remembering optional values may be missing.
  • Optional chaining and ?? are useful for safe access and fallback values.
  • Async functions return Promises; type them as Promise<T>.
  • Catch values should be checked before using properties.
  • DOM elements can be null; check before interacting.
  • TypeScript does not validate runtime data by itself.
  • Use npx tsc --noEmit to type-check without emitting files.
